tier_reason: speedtest-resize is an independent harness with public code (main.go, exec.go), but the epeg row comes from a single contributor pass on an unnamed 'Intel Core i7 3.4GHz' with no tool versions. Its only win is over 'convert -resize', which decodes the full 5616x3744 image and runs a convolution filter, while epeg decodes at 1/8 scale in the DCT domain and point-samples; against the equivalent ImageMagick mode (-define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail) epeg is slower, so the faster-than-ImageMagick claim fails and the evidence is C at most if kept.

corrections.claimed_speedup: speedtest-resize README, scenario run by contributor nono (3.4GHz Intel Core i7, Ubuntu 16.10, average over the first 10 JPEGs, one pass): epeg 0.079 s per file vs ImageMagick_resize ('convert -resize 150x150>') 0.568 s, 7.2x (derived from page data), but that ImageMagick command decodes the full 5616x3744 image and runs a convolution resize while epeg decodes at 1/8 scale in the DCT domain and point-samples. Against ImageMagick_thumbnail ('convert -define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail 150x150>'), which uses the same libjpeg DCT-domain downscale, epeg is slower: 0.079 s vs 0.057 s (ImageMagick 1.39x faster, derived from page data). The vips binding (0.070 s) is also faster than epeg; vipsthumbnail (0.115 s) and GraphicsMagick_thumbnail (0.172 s) are slower.
corrections.workload: speedtest-resize (Go driver main.go and exec.go): for each of the first 10 JPEGs (5616x3744) in a folder, spawn the tool, load, scale to a 150x100 thumbnail and write a JPEG; the time includes process start-up. epeg runs as 'epeg -m 150' (libjpeg scale_denom 8 with JDCT_IFAST, no fancy upsampling and no block smoothing, i.e. a 702x468 decode, then nearest-neighbour point sampling in _epeg_scale, JPEG quality 85). ImageMagick_resize runs 'convert -resize 150x150>' (full-resolution decode plus ImageMagick's default convolution filter); ImageMagick_thumbnail runs 'convert -define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail 150x150>' (DCT-domain downscale at decode, then a filtered resize).
corrections.baseline: ImageMagick convert -resize 150x150> (plain resize mode); ImageMagick's own -thumbnail mode with the jpeg:size hint is faster than epeg in the same table
corrections.hardware: 3.4GHz Intel Core i7 (model not stated), Ubuntu 16.10; scenario run by GitHub user nono and added to the README. epeg and ImageMagick versions not stated.
corrections.license: MIT-enna (Enlightenment MIT variant: COPYING requires publicly documented acknowledgment when the source is not published; COPYING-PLAIN is a non-binding plain-English note). Not OSI-approved.
corrections.caveats: Equivalent-work comparison fails: in the same speedtest-resize table ImageMagick's own thumbnail command ('convert -define jpeg:size=300x300 -thumbnail 150x150>'), which uses the same libjpeg DCT-domain downscale, takes 0.057 s per file against epeg's 0.079 s, and the vips binding takes 0.070 s. epeg only beats 'convert -resize 150x150>', which decodes the full 5616x3744 image and runs a convolution resize, while epeg decodes at 1/8 scale (JDCT_IFAST, no fancy upsampling) and then nearest-neighbour samples to 150x100, so it does much less work and gives a lower-quality thumbnail. The numbers are one pass over 10 files by a contributor (nono) on an unnamed Core i7 with process start-up included and no tool versions. The licence is the Enlightenment MIT variant (MIT-enna) with a public-acknowledgment clause, which is not OSI-approved. mattes/epeg is a maintained copy of Enlightenment's epeg, not a GitHub fork.

notes: Plainly: epeg loses to ImageMagick's -thumbnail with the jpeg:size hint in the same table (0.079 s vs 0.057 s per file) and to the vips binding (0.070 s); its 7.2x over 'convert -resize' comes from doing much less work (1/8-scale DCT decode with JDCT_IFAST, then nearest-neighbour sampling). If the orchestrator keeps it under the keep-and-document rule, use tier C, usability reference and the corrected caveats. Repo metadata checked on github.com: 274 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2023-04-05 (abandoned).

tier_reason: The libvips wiki Speed-and-memory-use table is the libvips maintainers' measurement, independent of both FFmpeg and ImageMagick, with public scripts in libvips/vips-bench (ffmpeg.sh, im7.sh, im.sh, benchmark.sh) and a named CPU (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04, run 12 Aug 2025). All tools are Ubuntu packages with no compiler or flags stated, so B, not A (same call as the GraphicsMagick entry in batch-16).

corrections.workload: libvips vips-bench (ffmpeg.sh vs im7.sh/im.sh, driver benchmark.sh): the ffmpeg 7.1.1 CLI reads the 10000x10000 8-bit RGB image as a strip TIFF (x-strip.tif; benchmark.sh notes ffmpeg does not support tiled TIFF), crops 100 px per edge (crop filter), scales to 90 percent with the scale filter at libswscale's default SWS_BICUBIC (ffmpeg.sh passes no flags), runs a 3x3 sharpen (kernel sum 8, divided by 8) through the convolution filter, which accepts planar formats only, and writes a TIFF. ImageMagick 7.1.1 reads the tiled TIFF with crop-on-load, resizes 90 percent with -filter triangle and convolves the same 3x3 kernel; its script also runs vipsheader twice inside the timed command. Quickest real time of five runs, OMP_NUM_THREADS=16.
corrections.claimed_speedup: libvips wiki table (AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04, run 12 Aug 2025): ffmpeg 7.1.1 2.06 s and 1338.36 MB peak vs magick 7.1.1 4.41 s / 1500.52 MB and convert 7.1.1 4.44 s / 1499.29 MB, 2.1x faster (derived from page data); the page's 'times slower than libvips' column reads ffmpeg 3.61 vs magick 7.74.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3955WX 16-core, Ubuntu 25.04 (run 12 Aug 2025 by the libvips maintainers)
corrections.license: LGPL-2.1-or-later (optional parts make the build GPL-2.0-or-later when configured with --enable-gpl, per LICENSE.md); libswscale and vf_convolution.c are LGPL
corrections.caveats: One trivial I/O-dominated test (the wiki says it flatters libvips), so the 2.1x mostly reflects TIFF reading and writing and pipeline overhead rather than swscale itself. The pipelines are not identical: ffmpeg reads the strip TIFF (it does not support tiled TIFF) and resamples with libswscale's default bicubic filter (a wider kernel than ImageMagick's triangle), while ImageMagick reads the tiled TIFF with crop-on-load, resizes with -filter triangle, and its script runs vipsheader twice inside the timed command. vips-bench issue 8 (homm, 2017, about Pillow) notes that libvips uses 4-point bilinear interpolation while ImageMagick and GraphicsMagick use convolution resizing, so resampling differs per program. Distribution packages with no compiler or flags. Already recorded entries (zimg, yuv2rgb) use libswscale as their baseline rather than ImageMagick. FFmpeg becomes GPL-2.0-or-later when configured with --enable-gpl.

notes: All numbers are on the wiki page in the ffmpeg, magick and convert rows. The record wrongly said ffmpeg read the tiled TIFF and used bilinear: ffmpeg.sh reads x-strip.tif and leaves libswscale at its SWS_BICUBIC default (libswscale/options.c, doc/scaler.texi in release/7.1), which is more resampling work than ImageMagick's triangle filter, so the difference does not favour ffmpeg. Metadata checked on github.com: GitHub mirror of git.ffmpeg.org, 64.7k stars, last commit 2026-10-03 (active).

tier_reason: pillow-perf is a well-known suite independent of OpenCV and ImageMagick (run by the Pillow-SIMD authors) with public code (testsuite/cases/cv2_scale.py, cv2_blur.py, wand_scale.py, wand_blur.py, run.py, auto/run.sh) and a named CPU (Core i5-4430), and the libvips wiki row (vips-bench opencv.cc vs im7.sh, Threadripper PRO 3955WX) is also independent; both use binary wheels or distro packages with no compiler or flags, so B, not A. Tier unchanged; the verdict is downgrade because part of the claim was overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: pillow-perf i5-4430 (Core i5-4430, Ubuntu 18.04.3; both libraries single-threaded via cv2.setNumThreads(1) and MAGICK_THREAD_LIMIT=1; median of 5 runs, 3 for ImageMagick blur) on a 2560x1600 RGB image, like-for-like rows (derived from page data): 2.14x upscale to 5478x3424, OpenCV INTER_LINEAR 57.74 ms vs ImageMagick 6.9 triangle 1007.63 ms (17.5x) and INTER_CUBIC 115.25 ms vs Catmull-Rom 1256.13 ms (10.9x); Gaussian blur radius 1 px 69.39 vs 675.34 ms (9.7x), 10 px 445.67 vs 1768.07 ms (4.0x), 30 px 1399.39 vs 4090.08 ms (2.9x). The downscale rows the record called bicubic (320x200: 5.41 vs 89.20 ms; 2048x1280: 48.20 vs 222.93 ms) are OpenCV INTER_AREA supersampling (the raw i5-4430.txt labels them 'sup'; the JSON files them under 'bic') against ImageMagick Catmull-Rom convolution, so they are not like for like. libvips wiki (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04): opencv 4.10 3.15 s vs magick 7.1.1 4.41 s and convert 7.1.1 4.44 s (1.4x, derived from page data). pillow-perf also shows OpenCV slower than ImageMagick at JPEG load (47.89 vs 27.38 ms) and save (56.70 vs 48.04 ms). The speedtest-resize opencv row (0.110 s vs ImageMagick_resize 0.568 s) uses go-opencv Resize with interpolation 0 (CV_INTER_NN, nearest neighbour) and is not comparable; ImageMagick_thumbnail (0.057 s) is faster there.
corrections.workload: pillow-perf testsuite (run.py default 2560x1600 RGB; cv2_scale.py vs wand_scale.py, cv2_blur.py vs wand_blur.py): in-memory resampling and Gaussian blur, single-threaded, no file I/O; OpenCV downscales use INTER_AREA and upscales (2.14x) use INTER_LINEAR, INTER_CUBIC and INTER_LANCZOS4, while ImageMagick uses triangle, catrom and lanczos at every size; blur uses the same window (1 + 2*ceil(2.5r)) and sigma r. libvips wiki (vips-bench opencv.cc vs im7.sh): load a 10000x10000 8-bit RGB tiled TIFF, crop 100 px per edge, resize to 90 percent (OpenCV's default INTER_LINEAR 4-point bilinear vs ImageMagick -filter triangle convolution), 3x3 sharpen, save.
corrections.baseline: ImageMagick (6.9 via the Wand binding, single-threaded, in pillow-perf; magick and convert 7.1.1 in the libvips Speed-and-memory-use table)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated: pillow-perf installs the opencv-python binary wheel (the data file says 'Opencv 4.1'; auto/run.sh pinned opencv-python 4.1.2.30 from Nov 2019 to Feb 2020) and ImageMagick from the system; the libvips wiki used the Ubuntu 25.04 opencv 4.10 package, with the driver compiled as 'g++ -g -Wall opencv.cc'.
corrections.caveats: The pillow-perf downscale cells filed as bicubic for OpenCV (26x16, 320x200, 2048x1280) are INTER_AREA supersampling runs (cv2_scale.py; the raw i5-4430.txt labels them 'sup') compared against ImageMagick Catmull-Rom convolution; pillow-perf's own page says comparing OpenCV's bicubic with correct convolution implementations is meaningless and that supersampling is a different method, so those 16.5x and 4.6x ratios are not like for like. The like-for-like pillow-perf rows are the 2.14x upscale (INTER_LINEAR vs triangle; INTER_CUBIC with a=-0.75 vs Catmull-Rom, both 4x4 support) and the Gaussian blur (same window and sigma), all single-threaded. The Lanczos row is OpenCV Lanczos4 (439.03 ms) against ImageMagick Lanczos3 (1495.61 ms), not like for like. OpenCV is slower than ImageMagick at JPEG load and save in the same file. The baseline is ImageMagick 6.9 from Ubuntu 18.04 (2020 run), and the suite is maintained by the Pillow-SIMD authors. In the libvips pipeline OpenCV's default 4-point bilinear does slightly less filtering than ImageMagick's triangle convolution at 0.9 scale; the test is I/O dominated, the wiki says it flatters libvips, and OpenCV is listed among systems that do not thread automatically. The speedtest-resize opencv row (go-opencv Resize with interpolation 0, nearest neighbour) is not comparable to ImageMagick_resize.

notes: Downgrade is for the overstated claim, not the tier: the upscale and blur rows and the libvips wiki row still support B. ImageMagick 6.9.7-4 and 6.8.9-9 do not appear in the data I opened (it says 'ImageMagick 6.9' and 'Opencv 4.1'); OpenCV 4.1.2 is consistent with the auto/run.sh pin history.
